title: Clean up file handle on interrupt, timeout
Close the lock file when lock() fails to get the lock
description:
filelock_lock() opens the lock file before it tries to lock it, but it only kept or closed the file descriptor when the lock succeeded. Every failed lock() call leaked one: a timeout = 0 call that finds the file locked, a timeout > 0 call that times out, a locking error, and on Unix an interrupt while waiting. A process that polls a busy lock accumulates descriptors until it hits the fd limit or select()'s FD_SETSIZE.

On Unix, close the descriptor on the no-lock return paths and before the error() calls in filelock_lock(). The wait in
filelock__interruptible() can longjmp out through error() or R_CheckUserInterrupt(), so it now runs under R_UnwindProtect(), which closes the descriptor and then continues the jump. The interrupt is still an interrupt. R_UnwindProtect() needs R 3.5.0, so Depends is now R (>= 3.5).

On Windows, close the handle on the timeout return path and before each filelock__error() call after CreateFileW(). The interrupt paths already closed it. The WAIT_FAILED paths now read GetLastError() before the cleanup calls, so the reported error code is not clobbered.

The new tests hold the lock from a child process and check that failed lock() calls do not leave the lock file open, for timeouts and for an interrupt. ps is added to Suggests for this.

Fixes r-lib/filelock#28.

title: unlock(remove = TRUE): delete the lock file on release, safely
description:
Lock files are never deleted today, so a cache that locks one file per entry ends up with hundreds of thousands of empty files that are not in use. This adds an option to delete a lock file when its lock is released, without the race that naive deletion causes, so lock files exist only while in use.

**Affects:** nothing unless `unlock(remove = TRUE)` is used; `lock()` also now re-checks the file it locked, which always passes when no one deletes lock files.

<details><summary>Technical details</summary>

Deleting a lock file while another process waits on it is unsafe: the waiter later gets its lock on the deleted file, while a newcomer creates and locks a new file at the same path, so both "hold" the lock. Now:

- `filelock_lock()` (`src/filelock-unix.c`): after acquiring, `filelock__same_file()` compares `fstat()` of the open file with `stat()` of the path (device and inode). If they differ, or the path is gone, it closes and starts over (the timeout restarts). `ESTALE` from `fcntl()` (NFS, file deleted by its holder) also starts over.
- `filelock_unlock(lock, remove)`: with `remove = TRUE`, an exclusive lock's last reference `unlink()`s the file before `close()`. Shared locks and nested references keep it. A crash leaves the file; the next `unlock(remove = TRUE)` on it deletes it.
- Windows: `remove` is ignored (a file other processes have open cannot be deleted there).

Tests: `remove` deletes only on the last exclusive release; a waiter whose file is deleted ends up holding the new file at the path (fails when the waiter runs the old code). Stress test outside the suite: 8 processes × 300 increments of a shared counter under the lock, deleting on every release: 2400/2400 in 3/3 runs; with the same-file check disabled the counter file ends up empty (two processes in the critical section) in 3/3 runs. Version 1.0.3.9002, so reproducible can require it.

</details>

title: Fix itimer state restoration in filelock
description:
Currently filelock restores the SIGALRM handler to its previous state but the itimer state is not restored. This can disrupt existing timers that were running before the filelock operation, such as R's profiling timer used by `Rprof()`.

The issue occurs because while filelock correctly saves and restores the signal handler using `sigaction()`, it doesn't save and restore the timer state when calling `setitimer()`. This means any existing timer gets lost when filelock sets its own timer for timeout handling.

## Changes Made

This PR adds minimal changes to properly save and restore the itimer state:

1. **Added global variable** `filelock_old_timer` to store the previous timer state
2. **Modified setitimer call** to capture existing timer state before setting new one
3. **Updated alarm callback** to restore both signal handler and timer state

```c
// Before: timer state was lost
setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, &timer, 0);

// After: timer state is preserved  
setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, &timer, &filelock_old_timer);
```

The alarm callback now restores both the signal handler and the timer:

```c
void filelock__alarm_callback (int signum) {
  /* Restore signal handler */
  sigaction(SIGALRM, &filelock_old_sa, 0);
  /* Restore timer state */
  setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, &filelock_old_timer, 0);
}
```

## Impact

This fix allows systems like R's profiling (`Rprof()`) to resume normal operation after filelock completes, as the profiling timer will be properly restored along with its interval settings. The handler will have missed some intervals during the filelock operation, but this is expected behavior since timer intervals are only a lower bound and handlers should account for this possibility.

Fixes #42.

title: Include lock file path in locking error messages
description:
## Problem

When locking fails, the error message does not say which lock file could not be opened or locked. This makes stale lock files (e.g. left behind by an interrupted `pak::pkg_install()`, see r-lib/pak#263) hard for users to find and remove.

## Changes

All locking error messages now include the lock file path, in backticks, and follow the tidyverse error style ("Can't", trailing full stop), within the constraints of raising errors from C without a cli dependency:

- Unix: ``Can't open lock file `<path>`: Permission denied.`` (and similarly for lock failures).
- Windows: `filelock__error()` now formats ``Can't open lock file `<path>`: Access is denied (Windows error 5).``, putting the problem statement before the error code and stripping the trailing CRLF of the system message.
- The ``File `<path>` already has a shared/exclusive lock.`` errors now name the file.
- Fixed the `utf8.c` caller of `filelock__error()` for the new signature.
- Added a regression test asserting the path appears in the error message when the lock file cannot be opened, and updated the snapshot test (with a path-scrubbing transform) for the new messages.
- NEWS entry.

Note: I could only compile and test the Unix implementation locally (macOS); the Windows code paths should be verified by CI.

Closes #30.

title: Add "Supported By Posit" badge to filelock website
description:
## Overview

This PR adds the "Supported by Posit" badge to the filelock website.

## Background

We've recently started adding a "Supported by Posit" badge across all Posit package websites to create a more cohesive brand presence. The badge appears on the far right of the top navigation bar or at the bottom of the hamburger menu. It links to Posit’s main website. @hadley is involved with this initiative.

The following websites already have the "Supported by Posit" badge: [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org), [Great Tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/articles/intro.html), [gt](https://gt.rstudio.com), [Plotnine](https://plotnine.org), [Pointblank](https://posit-dev.github.io/pointblank/), [pointblank](https://rstudio.github.io/pointblank/), and [Quarto](https://quarto.org).

See https://posit-dev.github.io/supported-by-posit/ for more information.

## Changes

- Added a line to `_pkgdown.yml` to include the JavaScript file
- Standardized indentation in `_pkgdown.yml`
